meta.title: LLM Training: From Pre-training to RLHF
meta.subtitle: A deep dive into how Large Language Models are trained

content.title: The Foundation
content.content: Pre-training is teaching an LLM to predict the next {term:token:token} given previous tokens. It's like teaching a child to read by showing them billions of sentences.

Objective: Learn general language patterns, facts, and reasoning abilities from massive text corpora.

Scale: Trillions of {term:token:tokens}, thousands of GPUs, weeks to months of training.

rows: Web text (Common Crawl), books, Wikipedia, code (GitHub)
Next token prediction (causal LM) or masked LM
Base model that can complete text but isn't instruction-following

explanation.template: Minimize the negative log {term:probability:probability} of predicting the correct next {term:token:token} given all previous tokens. The {term:weights:model weights θ} are updated via {term:gradient:gradient descent}.

content.title: What happens during training?
content.content:
1. Sample a batch of text sequences from {term:data:training data}
2. For each {term:token:token}, compute model's {term:probability:probability distribution} over vocabulary
3. Calculate {term:loss:cross-entropy loss} against ground truth
4. Backpropagate to compute {term:gradient:gradients}
5. Update {term:weights:weights} using optimizer (Adam, AdamW)

content.title: What the model learns
content.content:
• Syntax & Grammar: Proper sentence structure
• World Knowledge: Facts about entities, events, concepts
• Reasoning Patterns: Logical chains, analogies
• Code Understanding: Programming languages, APIs
• Multilinguality: Many languages from diverse web data

content.title: But there's a problem...
content.content:
The base model predicts likely continuations, not helpful responses.

Prompt: 'What is the capital of France?'
Base Model: 'What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Italy?...' (continues the pattern)

We need fine-tuning to make it assistant-like!

content.title: What is SFT?
content.content:
SFT = Teaching the model to follow instructions by showing it (instruction, response) pairs.

Unlike pre-training which uses raw text, SFT uses curated high-quality examples of how an assistant should behave.
Goal: Transform a text completion model into an instruction-following assistant.

content.title: Data Format
content.content:
Input: '[INST] What is machine learning? [/INST]'
Target: 'Machine learning is a subset of AI that enables systems to learn from data...'

The {term:loss:loss} is only computed on the response tokens, not the instruction.

explanation.template: Only the {term:token:tokens} in the response contribute to the {term:loss:loss}. The instruction provides context but isn't predicted.

content.title: Key Techniques
content.content:
• LoRA/QLoRA: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (freeze base, train adapters)
• Instruction Templates: Consistent format for prompts
• Chat Format: Multi-turn conversation structure
• Data Quality: More important than quantity

content.title: What SFT achieves
content.content:
✅ Follows instructions
✅ Answers questions directly
✅ Maintains consistent persona
✅ Formats outputs properly (code, lists, etc.)

content.title: But there are limitations...
content.content:
❌ Imitates, doesn't optimize: Copies annotator behavior, good or bad
❌ Distribution mismatch: May struggle outside training distribution
❌ No preference learning: Doesn't know which of two good answers is better

This is where RLHF comes in!

content.title: What is RLHF?
content.content:
RLHF = Using human preferences to train a {term:reward:reward model}, then optimizing the LLM to maximize that {term:reward:reward} while staying close to the SFT model.

It's teaching the model not just what to say, but how well to say it.

The Three Steps:
1. SFT - Create initial instruction-following model
2. Reward Model - Train model to predict human preferences
3. RL Optimization - Optimize {term:policy:policy} against {term:reward:reward} with {term:kl:KL} constraint

content.title: Why not just use more SFT data?
content.content:
• Human preferences are comparative: 'A is better than B' is easier to annotate than writing perfect responses
• SFT copies behavior; RLHF optimizes for quality
• RLHF learns subtle preferences that are hard to explicitly write down

content.title: The Classic RLHF Algorithm
content.content: PPO is the standard RL algorithm used in RLHF. It updates the {term:policy:policy} to maximize {term:reward:reward} while constraining how much the {term:policy:policy} can change in each step.

explanation.template: Maximize {term:reward:reward} (via {term:advantage:advantage}) while keeping the {term:policy:policy} close to the {term:reference:reference model} using a {term:kl:KL divergence} penalty.

content.title: Key Components
content.content:
• r(θ): Ratio of new to old {term:policy:policy} {term:probability:probabilities}
• {term:advantage:A}: How much better the action is than expected
• clip: Prevents too large updates
• {term:kl:KL} penalty: Prevents model from drifting too far from SFT

content.title: A Simpler Alternative
content.content: GRPO (from DeepSeek) eliminates the need for a separate {term:value:value function} by computing {term:advantage:advantages} relative to a group of samples for the same prompt.

explanation.template: Instead of learning a {term:value:value function}, GRPO samples multiple responses per prompt and uses the group's {term:reward:reward} statistics to compute relative {term:advantage:advantages}.

content.title: Why GRPO is Popular
content.content:
• Simpler implementation (no critic network)
• Used by DeepSeek for their R1 model
• Works well with verifiable rewards (math, code)
• Easier to scale

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: A number that tells us how wrong the model is. Lower {term:loss:loss} = better predictions. Training tries to minimize this.
In LLMs, typically cross-entropy: {term:loss:L} = −Σ log {term:probability:P}(correct {term:token:token}). Measures negative log-likelihood of ground truth.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
If model predicts 'Paris' with 90% confidence and it's correct:
{term:loss:L} = −log(0.9) ≈ 0.105 (low, good!)

If model predicts 'Paris' with 10% confidence:
{term:loss:L} = −log(0.1) ≈ 2.3 (high, bad!)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The direction to nudge {term:weights:weights} to reduce {term:loss:loss}. Like a compass pointing downhill.
{term:gradient:∇}L = vector of partial derivatives of {term:loss:loss} w.r.t. each {term:weights:weight}. Points in direction of steepest increase.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
If {term:gradient:∇}L = [0.1, -0.2, 0.05], we update weights:
{term:weights:θ_new} = {term:weights:θ} - lr × {term:gradient:∇}L
= {term:weights:θ} - 0.001 × [0.1, -0.2, 0.05]

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: All the numbers inside the neural network that get learned during training. The 'brain' of the model.
{term:weights:θ} ∈ ℝⁿ where n = billions for modern LLMs. Includes embeddings, attention weights, MLP weights, layer norms.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
LLaMA-7B: 7 billion {term:weights:parameters}
GPT-4: ~1.7 trillion {term:weights:parameters}

Stored as fp16/bf16 floats, so 7B params ≈ 14GB

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The text the model learns from. Quality and diversity of {term:data:data} directly impacts model capabilities.

sections.title: In Pre-training
sections.content: Trillions of {term:token:tokens} from web, books, code. Common Crawl, Wikipedia, Stack Overflow, GitHub.

sections.title: In SFT
sections.content: Curated (instruction, response) pairs. 10K-1M examples, human-written or AI-generated.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: A chunk of text - could be a word, part of a word, or a character. LLMs process text as sequences of {term:token:tokens}.
Output of tokenizer (BPE, SentencePiece). Vocabulary typically 32K-100K {term:token:tokens}.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
'Hello, world!' → ['Hello', ',', ' world', '!'] (4 {term:token:tokens})
'Unbelievable' → ['Un', 'believ', 'able'] (3 {term:token:tokens})

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: How confident the model is about a {term:token:token}. Ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), sums to 1 over vocabulary.
{term:probability:P}({term:token:t}|context) = softmax(logits)[{term:token:t}]. Distribution over vocabulary at each position.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
'The capital of France is' →
{term:probability:P}('Paris') = 0.92
{term:probability:P}('Lyon') = 0.03
{term:probability:P}('Berlin') = 0.01
...

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: A score that says how 'good' a response is. Comes from a reward model trained on human preferences.
{term:reward:R}: (prompt, response) → ℝ. Higher = more preferred. Trained to predict which response humans prefer.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Prompt: 'Explain gravity'

Response A (detailed, accurate): {term:reward:R} = 0.85
Response B (brief, vague): {term:reward:R} = 0.32

RL training maximizes expected {term:reward:R}.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The LLM itself, viewed as a function that takes prompts and produces responses. In RL terms, the 'agent' that chooses actions ({term:token:tokens}).
{term:policy:π}(response|prompt) = Π {term:probability:P}({term:token:t_i}|prompt, {term:token:t_<i}). The full distribution over responses.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
{term:policy:π_θ}('Hello!' | 'Hi') = 0.05
{term:policy:π_θ}('Hi there!' | 'Hi') = 0.12

RL training changes {term:weights:θ} to increase {term:probability:probability} of high-{term:reward:reward} responses.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Predicts how much total {term:reward:reward} we expect from a given state. Used as a baseline to reduce variance in RL.
{term:value:V}(s) = 𝔼[Σ {term:reward:R}_t | s_0 = s]. Expected return starting from state s.

sections.title: In RLHF
sections.content: Often a separate model (critic) that predicts {term:reward:reward} for partial responses. Not needed in GRPO!

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: Measures how different two {term:probability:probability} distributions are. Used to keep the RL {term:policy:policy} close to the SFT model.
{term:kl:KL}(P||Q) = Σ P(x) log(P(x)/Q(x)). Always ≥ 0, equals 0 only if P = Q.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.content: Without {term:kl:KL} penalty, RL might find 'reward hacking' - responses that get high {term:reward:reward} but are nonsensical. {term:kl:KL} keeps model grounded in SFT behavior.

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: How much better an action is compared to the average. Positive = better than expected, negative = worse.
{term:advantage:A}(s,a) = Q(s,a) - {term:value:V}(s). Or in GRPO: normalized {term:reward:reward} within a group.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Group of 4 responses with {term:reward:rewards} [0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.3]
Mean = 0.45, Std = 0.23

{term:advantage:A} for response with R=0.8:
= (0.8 - 0.45) / 0.23 = 1.52 (strongly positive)

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content: The SFT model we started with, frozen. Used as an anchor to prevent the RL {term:policy:policy} from going crazy.
{term:reference:π_ref} = copy of {term:policy:π} before RL training. {term:kl:KL}({term:policy:π}||{term:reference:π_ref}) penalizes drift.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.content: If {term:policy:π} says 'Great answer!' to everything (gets high {term:reward:reward}), {term:kl:KL} penalty kicks in because {term:reference:π_ref} wouldn't do that.
